results.title: Maximal tensor rank is at most twice the generic rank (Blekherman–Teitler)
results.summary: Let ds be any list of dimensions, and consider complex tensors (Holor ℂ ds) with the product topology on HolorIndex ds → ℂ. Suppose r is a generic rank: there is an open dense set U of tensors, all of CP rank exactly r. Suppose R is the maximal rank: R is the largest CP rank of any tensor of format ds. Then R ≤ 2r. This is [BT15, Theorem 1] (Blekherman–Teitler), as formalized in formal-conjectures (FormalConjectures/Arxiv/0805.3777/TensorRank.lean).
results.notes: The source is G. Blekherman and Z. Teitler, "On maximum, typical and generic ranks", Math. Ann. 362 (2015), 1021–1031, doi:10.1007/s00208-014-1150-3, arXiv:1402.2371, Theorem 1. It states that the maximum rank is at most twice the generic rank for any nondegenerate irreducible variety. The case here is the Segre variety, i.e. tensors. The upstream file is FormalConjectures/Arxiv/0805.3777/TensorRank.lean, which builds on Friedland, LAA 436 (2012), arXiv:0805.3777. It has no formal_proof link for this item, and I know of no earlier Lean proof.

results.title: Gowers–Long lower bound: F(k²) ≥ k³ for 2-increasing sequences of triples
results.summary: Say that a triple a = (a_1,a_2,a_3) is 2-less than b = (b_1,b_2,b_3) if a_i < b_i for at least two coordinates i. A finite sequence of triples is 2-increasing if every earlier term is 2-less than every later term. Let F(n) be the largest length of a 2-increasing sequence of triples with all coordinates in {1,...,n}. (Formally, F(n) is the sSup in ℕ of the set of such lengths.) If n is a perfect square then (√n)^3 ≤ F(n), i.e. F(k^2) ≥ k^3 for every natural number k.
results.notes: The source is W. T. Gowers and J. Long, "The length of an s-increasing sequence of r-tuples", arXiv:1609.08688, published in Combinatorics, Probability and Computing 30 (2021), 686–721. Proposition 1.4 states F(n) ≤ n^2 for all n, and F(n) ≥ n^{3/2} when n is a perfect square, using the lexicographic construction of triples ((a,b),(a,c),(b,c)). The result is known and elementary. In formal-conjectures, both the pinned checkout and the latest upstream HEAD (d9ce556, 2026-10-17) still leave `maximalLength_ge_of_isSquare` as `sorry`. The upper bound `maximalLength_le` is already proved upstream. I found no existing Lean proof of the lower bound.

results.title: Supermultiplicativity of F gives arbitrarily large m with F(m) ≥ m^α (Gowers–Long)
results.summary: Let F(n) be the largest length of a sequence of triples in {1,…,n}^3 that is 2-increasing: every earlier triple is strictly smaller than every later one in at least two of the three coordinates. Let n > 1 be a natural number and e a real number with F(n) = n^e. Then (m : ℝ)^e ≤ F(m) for arbitrarily large natural numbers m, i.e. ∃ᶠ m in atTop.
results.notes: W. T. Gowers and J. Long, "The length of an s-increasing sequence of r-tuples", arXiv:1609.08688; Combinatorics, Probability and Computing 30 (2021), 686–721. Section 1 notes that F is supermultiplicative, F(mn) ≥ F(m)F(n), using the lexicographic product of sequences. So F(n) = n^α implies F(n^k) ≥ n^{αk}, which gives arbitrarily large m with F(m) ≥ m^α. This is the upstream statement `maximalLength_pow`, which is tagged "research solved" and was proved upstream only by sorry. I found no existing Lean formalization.

results.title: Finite free Stam inequality in degree 2 (First Proof, Problem 4, n = 2): it holds with equality
results.summary: Let p and q be monic real polynomials of degree 2, each having 2 real roots counted with multiplicity. Let p ⊞_2 q be their finite additive convolution, Σ_{k=0}^{2} c_k x^{2-k} with c_k = Σ_{i+j=k} (2-i)!(2-j)!/(2!(2-k)!) a_i b_j, where a_i and b_j are the coefficients of x^{2-i} in p and x^{2-j} in q. For a monic polynomial with simple roots λ_1,…,λ_n, set Φ_n(p) = Σ_i (Σ_{j≠i} 1/(λ_i-λ_j))^2, and set Φ_n(p) = ∞ when p has a repeated root. Then, in [0,∞], 1/Φ_2(p) + 1/Φ_2(q) ≤ 1/Φ_2(p ⊞_2 q). In fact equality always holds.
results.notes: The problem is First Proof (Abouzaid, Blumberg, Hairer, Kileel, Kolda, Nelson, Spielman, Srivastava, Ward, Weinberger, Williams), arXiv:2602.05192v2, Problem 4: the finite free Stam / harmonic-mean inequality for ⊞_n. ⊞_n is the finite free additive convolution of Marcus–Spielman–Srivastava ("Finite free convolutions of polynomials"; "Interlacing families II"). The general statement was answered affirmatively by the First Proof solutions. It was formalized in Lean 4 by FrenzyMath's Archon in the repository frenzymath/Archon-FirstProof-Results, file FirstProof/FirstProof4/Problem4.lean, theorem harmonic_mean_inequality_full, for all n ≥ 2 with zero sorrys according to its README. Upstream links that file as `formal_proof` on `four`. The n = 2 case is an elementary identity: ⊞_2 adds discriminants (second cumulants), so equality holds.

results.title: Γ_{3⊕3} (equal-sign pairs in S₃ × S₃) is not 2-generated
results.summary: Let Γ = Γ_{3⊕3} = {(σ₁, σ₂) ∈ S₃ × S₃ : sgn σ₁ = sgn σ₂}. In the formal statement Γ is the kernel of (σ₁,σ₂) ↦ sgn σ₁ · sgn σ₂⁻¹. For all h₁, h₂ ∈ Γ, the subgroup of Γ generated by {h₁, h₂} is not all of Γ. So Γ is not 2-generated, which is the rank-3 claim Fernandes records in arXiv:2605.12342.
results.notes: V. H. Fernandes, "Groups of permutations that are even on maximal proper subsets, and related monoids", arXiv:2605.12342 (2026). It states, as a GAP computation, that Γ3⊕3, Γ4⊕3 and Γ4⊕4 are not 2-generated, so rank(Γ3⊕3) = 3, and gives Conjecture 1 for all other (m, n). It also follows from elementary group theory: Γ3⊕3 is the generalized dihedral group Dih(C3×C3), and any 2-generated subgroup of it has order at most 9. Existing Lean work: K. Kitamura, github.com/KitaKen1/fernandes-conjecture-1-lean, proves only the main conjecture_1 (the non-exceptional cases are 2-generated), not the rank-3 exceptions. Upstream formal-conjectures main (checked 2026-10-17) still has `sorry` for conjecture_1.variants.rank_3_3.

results.title: The Poisson conjecture fails in dimension three
results.summary: Let K be a field of characteristic zero and P_3(K) = K[x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2,y_3] with the canonical Poisson bracket {f,g} = sum_i (d_{x_i} f d_{y_i} g - d_{y_i} f d_{x_i} g). Then some K-algebra endomorphism phi of P_3(K) is not bijective even though it preserves the bracket on generators ({phi(v), phi(w)} = {v, w} for all variables v, w). So PC_3 (every Poisson endomorphism of P_3(K) is an automorphism) is false. Formally: for every field K with CharZero K, ¬ PoissonConjectureFor K 3.
results.notes: [AvdE07] K. Adjamagbo and A. van den Essen, arXiv:math/0608009, Acta Math. Vietnam. 32 (2007): defines PC_n (Notations 5), Lemma 2 (preserving brackets on generators suffices), and Theorem 7 (JC_{2n} ⇒ PC_n ⇒ DC_n ⇒ JC_n). [Alp26] L. Alpöge (2026): counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture in dimension 3. The upstream formal-conjectures file FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/JacobianConjecture.lean formalizes a variant G with Jacobian determinant 1 that is not injective (det_jacobian_G, aeval_G_eq). Upstream FormalConjectures/Arxiv/math.0608009/PoissonConjecture.lean marks dimension_three as "research solved" with a sorry proof, no formal_proof link, and a docstring describing exactly this cotangent-lift argument. [Lon26] C. D. Long, arXiv:2608.23777, settles PC_2 and is not relevant to n=3.

results.title: The Jacobian conjecture in dimension 2n implies the Poisson conjecture in dimension n
results.summary: Let K be a field of characteristic zero and n a natural number. Suppose the Jacobian conjecture holds in 2n variables over K: every polynomial map F : K^{2n} -> K^{2n} whose Jacobian determinant is a unit of K[x_1,...,x_{2n}] has a polynomial two-sided compositional inverse. Then every K-algebra endomorphism phi of K[x_1..x_n, y_1..y_n] that preserves the canonical Poisson bracket {f,g} = sum_i (d_{x_i} f d_{y_i} g - d_{y_i} f d_{x_i} g) on the generators, i.e. {phi(X_v), phi(X_w)} = {X_v, X_w} for all v, w, is bijective. (Adjamagbo and van den Essen, arXiv math/0608009, Theorems 1 and 7.)
results.notes: K. Adjamagbo and A. van den Essen, "On the equivalence of the Jacobian, Dixmier and Poisson conjectures in any characteristic", arXiv math/0608009, published as "A proof of the equivalence of the Dixmier, Jacobian and Poisson conjectures", Acta Math. Vietnam. 32 (2007) 205-214. Theorem 1 / Theorem 7 there state JC_{2n} ⇒ PC_n ⇒ DC_n ⇒ JC_n; JC_{2n} ⇒ PC_n is the step proved here. Related: Bass-Connell-Wright 1982 (DC_n ⇒ JC_n); Tsuchimoto and Belov-Kanel-Kontsevich (JC_{2n} ⇒ DC_n). Upstream records JC as false in dimension 3 (Alpöge 2026) and PC_2 as false (Long 2026), so the hypothesis here is false for n ≥ 2 and the case that still matters, JC_2 ⇒ PC_1, is nontrivial. Upstream has no formal_proof link for this item.

results.summary: There is a strictly increasing sequence m : ℕ → ℕ with two properties. First, it is "genuinely sublacunary": for some c > 0, m(n+1)/m(n) ≥ 1 + c/log n for all sufficiently large n. Second, for every irrational ξ, the points ξ·m(n) mod 1 are dense in ℝ/ℤ.

results.title: The p-adic Littlewood conjecture for real quadratic irrationals
results.summary: Let p be a prime and ξ a real number whose minimal polynomial over ℚ has degree 2. Then inf over integers q ≥ 1 of q · |q|_p · ‖qξ‖ is 0. Here ‖·‖ is the distance to the nearest integer, |·|_p is the p-adic absolute value, and the infimum is the real sInf of the set {q · padicNorm p q · distToNearestInt(qξ) : q ∈ ℕ, q ≥ 1}.
results.notes: de Mathan, B. and Teulié, O., "Problèmes diophantiens simultanés", Monatshefte für Mathematik 143 (2004), 229–245. They proved the p-adic Littlewood conjecture for quadratic irrationals, in a stronger form with a log factor. The problem is stated as Problem 10.8 in Bugeaud, "Distribution modulo one and Diophantine approximation" (CUP, 2012), Chapter 10. The elementary Pell/units argument used here is the standard proof of the quadratic case. I found no prior Lean formalization: there is no formal_proof attribute on Bugeaud08.problem_10_8.variants.quadratic, nothing in Mathlib, and the related formal_conjectures statement LittlewoodConjecture.padic_littlewood_conjecture is open and sorried.

results.title: The set of Mahler Z-numbers is countable, so its Hausdorff dimension is 0, which is less than 1
results.summary: A Z-number is a real ξ > 0 such that the fractional part {ξ (3/2)^n} lies in [0, 1/2) for every integer n ≥ 1. The set Z of all Z-numbers has Hausdorff dimension < 1, i.e. dimH {ξ : ℝ | IsZNumber ξ} < 1 in ℝ≥0∞. Flatto, Lagarias and Pollington (1995) proved this result, recorded in Bugeaud, Problem 10.9. We prove something stronger, going back to Mahler (1968): Z is countable, so dimH Z = 0.
results.notes: Mahler, K. "An unsolved problem on the powers of 3/2", J. Austral. Math. Soc. 8 (1968) 313-321: shows each interval [k, k+1) contains at most one Z-number, so the set of Z-numbers is countable (hence of Lebesgue measure 0 and Hausdorff dimension 0). Flatto, Lagarias and Pollington, "On the range of fractional parts {ξ(p/q)^n}", Acta Arith. 70 (1995) 125-147, credited by the upstream docstring; for this particular set their result is weaker than Mahler's countability. Bugeaud, "Distribution modulo one and Diophantine approximation" (CUP 2012), Ch. 10, Problem 10.9. I know of no prior Lean formalization: the upstream formal_conjectures statement is `sorry` with no formal_proof link, and Mathlib has no Z-number results.

results.title: Mahler's Z-numbers form a Lebesgue-null set
results.summary: A Z-number is a real number ξ > 0 such that the fractional part {ξ (3/2)^n} lies in [0, 1/2) for every integer n ≥ 1. The set of Z-numbers has Lebesgue measure zero (Mahler 1968; Bugeaud, Distribution modulo one and Diophantine approximation, Problem 10.9, measure-zero variant). Formally: MeasureTheory.volume {ξ : ℝ | IsZNumber ξ} = 0.
results.notes: K. Mahler, "An unsolved problem on the powers of 3/2", J. Austral. Math. Soc. 8 (1968) 313-321: at most one Z-number in each interval [k, k+1) (n ≥ 0 normalization), so Z-numbers are countable, with counting function O(x^0.7). This gives measure zero. Y. Bugeaud, Distribution Modulo One and Diophantine Approximation (CUP 2012), Ch. 10, Problem 10.9. Flatto–Lagarias–Pollington, Acta Arith. 70 (1995), is the source of the related dimH variant. I know of no earlier Lean formalization: the upstream formal-conjectures item is a `sorry` with no formal_proof link. I could not search GitHub because session access is limited to configured repositories.

results.title: The fractional parts of (3/2)^n have infinitely many accumulation points
results.summary: Let r_n = {(3/2)^n} be the fractional part of (3/2)^n for n = 0, 1, 2, .... Call x an accumulation point of (r_n) if x lies in the closure of {r_n : n ∈ ℕ} \ {x}. Then the set of accumulation points of (r_n) is infinite. (Vijayaraghavan's theorem, cited in Kuipers–Niederreiter, Uniform Distribution of Sequences, Ch. 1.)
results.notes: T. Vijayaraghavan, "On the fractional parts of the powers of a number", J. London Math. Soc. 15 (1940), 159–160, proves that {(p/q)^n}, and in particular {(3/2)^n}, has infinitely many limit points. Kuipers & Niederreiter, Uniform Distribution of Sequences (1974), Ch. 1 notes cite it in the source referenced by the upstream file. Upstream google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (main, checked 2026-10-17) still has `sorry` for this theorem, and I know of no previous Lean proof.

results.title: Grechuk's example: 1117175146 is not a prime plus at most three powers of two
results.summary: Let N = 1117175146. There is no prime p and no multiset of at most three natural numbers e_1, ..., e_k (k ≤ 3, repetitions allowed) with N = p + 2^{e_1} + ... + 2^{e_k}. Formally: 1117175146 ∉ sumPrimeAndTwoPows 3, where sumPrimeAndTwoPows k = { p + Σ_{e ∈ pows} 2^e : p prime, pows a multiset of naturals with card pows ≤ k }.
results.notes:

The local problems.yaml lists problem 10 with status open and formalized "yes", with no Lean proof noted for this example.

results.title: Erdős Problem 1000: liminf φ_A(k)/n_k = 0 forces limsup φ_A(k)/n_k = 1
results.summary: Let n_0 < n_1 < n_2 < ... be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers. Let φ_A(k) be the number of integers 1 ≤ m ≤ n_k such that n_k / gcd(m, n_k) divides no n_j with j < k. Put r_k = φ_A(k)/n_k. If liminf_{k→∞} r_k = 0, then limsup_{k→∞} r_k = 1. (Erdős [Er64b], recorded as erdosproblems.com/1000.)
results.notes: The result is Erdős, P., "Problems and results on diophantine approximations", Compositio Math. 16 (1964), 52-65 [Er64b]: if liminf φ_A(k)/n_k = 0 then limsup φ_A(k)/n_k = 1. The function φ_A was introduced by Cassels, "Some metrical theorems in Diophantine approximation. I", Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. (1950) [Ca50b]. Cassels's existence result (liminf of the Cesàro averages equal to 0) shows the hypothesis can hold. Haight's PhD thesis [Ha] settled the main problem: the averages can tend to 0. The problem is erdosproblems.com/1000, listed as "proved (Lean)". That status refers to the main problem, whose existing formalization is https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1000.lean. That file covers only the main existence theorem, not the limsup_eq_one variant.

results.title: Erdős Problem 1000: φ_A(k)/n_k does not tend to 0
results.summary: Let n_0 < n_1 < n_2 < ... be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers. Let φ_A(k) be the number of integers 1 ≤ m ≤ n_k such that n_k / gcd(m, n_k) divides none of the earlier terms n_j with j < k. Then φ_A(k)/n_k does not tend to 0 as k → ∞. (Erdős [Er64b], erdosproblems.com/1000.)
results.notes: Erdős, Problems and results on diophantine approximations, Compositio Math. 1964 [Er64b], where Erdős proves that lim φ_A(k)/n_k ≠ 0 and that liminf = 0 forces limsup = 1. Cassels [Ca50b] introduced φ_A. Haight solved the main question. erdosproblems.com/1000 lists the problem as "proved (Lean)"; that formal proof (plby/lean-proofs src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1000.lean) covers only Haight's main theorem. math0 had already committed a proof of upstream erdos_1000.variants.limsup_eq_one (lean/Math0/ErdosProblems/Erdos1000_erdos_1000_variants_limsup_eq_one.lean), and this result follows from it directly. results.title: Erdős Problem 1008: every graph with m edges has a C4-free subgraph with at least √m/2 edges
results.summary: There is a constant c > 0 such that for every finite type V and every simple graph G on V, some subgraph H ≤ G contains no copy of the 4-cycle C4 and satisfies c · m^{1/2} ≤ |E(H)|, where m = |E(G)|. (Erdős, [Er71], called this bound "trivial" and asked for m^{2/3}.) We prove it with c = 1/2.
results.notes: The source is Erdős [Er71], "Some unsolved problems in graph theory and combinatorial analysis" (1971), which notes that ≫ m^{1/2} is trivial and asks for m^{2/3}. The m^{2/3} bound was proved by Conlon, Fox and Sudakov [CFS14b], "Large subgraphs without complete bipartite graphs" (arXiv:1401.6711), and Hunter gave a simpler proof in the erdosproblems forum. The main statement is formalized in Lean at https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1008.lean (Aristotle / Boris Alexeev), with constant 1/2 and exponent 2/3, and erdosproblems.com lists 1008 as "proved (Lean)". The exponent-1/2 variant follows immediately from that formalized result. The folklore argument used here (max degree versus maximum matching, m ≤ 2Δν) is standard.

results.title: Rademacher's theorem: ⌊n²/4⌋+1 edges force ⌊n/2⌋ triangles
results.summary: For every n ∈ ℕ and every simple graph G on the vertex set Fin n with exactly ⌊n²/4⌋ + 1 edges, G contains at least ⌊n/2⌋ triangles (3-cliques).
results.notes: Rademacher (1941, unpublished, reported by Erdős): a graph with ⌊n²/4⌋+1 edges has at least ⌊n/2⌋ triangles. Erdős, "On a theorem of Rademacher-Turán", Illinois J. Math. 6 (1962) 122-127, proves t⌊n/2⌋ for t < cn. Lovász–Simonovits (1976) and Nikiforov–Khadzhiivanov, C. R. Acad. Bulgare Sci. (1981), settle the case t < ⌊n/2⌋ (erdosproblems #1010, status: proved). An existing Lean 4 formalization of the general statement, which implies this variant at t = 1, is plby/lean-proofs src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos1010.lean (commit 8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e, theorem erdos_1010 at L612). It is linked through the formal_proof attribute on Erdos1010.erdos_1010 in /home/user/math0/lean/.lake/packages/formal_conjectures/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/1010.lean.

results.title: Erdős 1026: no constant c > 1 is admissible (Cambie's construction)
results.summary: Call c admissible if for every ε > 0, for all sufficiently large n, every sequence x_1,...,x_n of distinct positive reals has a monotone (non-decreasing or non-increasing) subsequence whose sum is at least (c − ε)/√n · Σ_i x_i. Then every admissible constant satisfies c ≤ 1, i.e. 1 is an upper bound of the set of admissible constants.
results.notes:
- Erdős, "Some unsolved problems in graph theory and combinatorial analysis" (1971) [Er71]: the original problem.
- erdosproblems.com/1026 forum: van Doorn's precise formulation, and Cambie's construction showing c ≤ 1.
- Tidor, Wang and Yang, arXiv:1608.04153 [TWY16], and Wagner, J. Graph Theory 2017 [Wa17]: the weighted Erdős–Szekeres theorem, which gives c ≥ 1 and hence c = 1.
- Hanani 1957 [Ha57]: c ≥ 1/√2.
- Steele 1995 [St95].
- Existing Lean formalization by Aristotle and Boris Alexeev: https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1026.lean. Its theorem `c_opt_eq_k_div_sq_add_a` gives the exact c_opt(n) for all n, which implies the upper bound. erdosproblems problems.yaml lists the status as "solved (Lean)", last updated 2025-12-12.
- Background: Tao's blog post https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2025/12/08/the-story-of-erdos-problem-126/.

results.title: Erdős 1048: the component of {|zⁿ| ≤ 1} containing 0 has diameter exactly 2
results.summary: For every natural number n ≥ 1, the connected component containing 0 of the level set {z ∈ ℂ : |zⁿ| ≤ 1} has (extended) diameter exactly 2. So the Erdős–Herzog–Piranian bound, which says the component containing 0 has diameter ≥ 2 when all roots lie in |z| ≤ r ≤ 1/2, is attained by f(z) = zⁿ.
results.notes:
- Erdős, P., Herzog, F. and Piranian, G., "Metric properties of polynomials", J. Analyse Math. 6 (1958), 125–148. This is the source of the diam ≥ 2 bound for 0 ≤ r ≤ 1/2 and of the remark that zⁿ shows it is sharp.
- Pommerenke, Ch., "On metric properties of complex polynomials", Michigan Math. J. (1961), 97–115.
- erdosproblems.com/1048: status "disproved (Lean)" as of 2026-01-27.
- The existing Lean proof at https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1048.lean (Aristotle / Boris Alexeev) covers only the main disproof, `not_erdos_1048`, through Pommerenke's zⁿ − rⁿ example with r > 1. It does not prove `erdos_1048.variants.diam_ge_two_is_best`.

results.title: Cliques in the non-commuting graph have at most [G : Z(G)] vertices
results.summary: Let G be a group and let Γ(G) be its non-commuting graph: the vertices are the elements of G, and g and h are adjacent iff gh ≠ hg. If the centre Z(G) has finite index n = [G : Z(G)], then Γ(G) contains no complete subgraph on n + 1 vertices (Lean: `(nonCommutingGraph G).CliqueFree ((Subgroup.center G).index + 1)` under `[(Subgroup.center G).FiniteIndex]`). This is the remark Neumann (1976) made in answering Erdős Problem 1098.
results.notes: B. H. Neumann, "A problem of Paul Erdős on groups", J. Austral. Math. Soc. Ser. A 21 (1976), 467–472. It proves that Γ(G) has no infinite clique iff [G:Z(G)] < ∞, and remarks that a clique has at most [G:Z(G)] vertices. erdosproblems.com/1098 lists the problem as "proved (Lean)" (problems.yaml, 2026-05-02). The existing Lean formalization is plby/lean-proofs, src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1098.lean, which is linked as formal_proof on upstream erdos_1098. Its theorem `erdos1098` contains the same coset-injection bound S.card ≤ Nat.card (G ⧸ center G) for pairwise non-commuting finsets under finite index, and `IsFIZGroup.isPEGroup` uses the same argument.

results.title: Erdős–Wetzel theorem: if ℵ₁ < 𝔠, families of entire functions with countably many values at each point are countable
results.summary: Assume ℵ₁ < 𝔠. Let F be a set of entire functions ℂ → ℂ such that for every z₀ ∈ ℂ the set of values {f(z₀) : f ∈ F} is countable. Then F is countable. (Formally, the hypothesis ℵ_1 < 𝔠 is stated in an arbitrary universe `Cardinal.{u_1}`.)
results.notes:
- Erdős, P., "An interpolation problem associated with the continuum hypothesis", Michigan Math. J. 11 (1964), 9–10. This is the original theorem: ¬CH implies the family is countable, and CH gives an uncountable counterexample.
- Hayman, W. K., Research problems in function theory (1974), Problem 2.46.
- Kumar–Shelah, Fund. Math. 2017, and Schilhan–Weinert, J. London Math. Soc. 2024. These give the independence of the general-cardinal problem.
- Earlier formalizations:
  - plby/lean-proofs (Boris Alexeev; Codex/GPT), src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos1119.lean at commit 8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e. It proves easy_case and `erdos_1119` (ℵ_1 < 𝔠 → pointwise-countable entire family is countable), and aliases it to `erdos_1119.variants.erdos_wetzel`.
  - Collin Yuanjie Ren, Lean proof of the full Wetzel/CH biconditional (github.com/CollinYuanjieRen/awards, jsp-000930-cyr). It is credited in the erdosproblems.com formal_status note, and the formalized state there is "yes".
  - L. C. Paulson, "Wetzel's Problem and the Continuum Hypothesis", Isabelle AFP (2022).

results.title: Goodman–Goodman covering theorem for balls in ℝ^d (Erdős 1121, higher-dimensional variant)
results.summary: Let d, n be natural numbers, c_1,…,c_n points of ℝ^d and r_1,…,r_n > 0. Suppose that for every nonzero v ∈ ℝ^d and every t ∈ ℝ, if the hyperplane {p : ⟨v,p⟩ = t} meets none of the closed balls B_i = B̄(c_i, r_i), then either ⟨v,c_i⟩ < t for all i or ⟨v,c_i⟩ > t for all i. Then there is z ∈ ℝ^d with ⋃_i B_i ⊆ B̄(z, R), where R = Σ_i r_i.
results.notes: The result is Goodman, A. W. and Goodman, R. E., "A circle covering theorem", Amer. Math. Monthly 52 (1945), 494–498. The upstream docstring notes that their proof generalises to higher dimensions. Hadwiger, "Nonseparable convex systems", Amer. Math. Monthly 54 (1947), 583–585, extends it to convex bodies. Bezdek and Litvak, "Packing convex bodies by cylinders", Discrete Comput. Geom. (2016), 725–738, give an alternative proof. erdosproblems.com/1121 lists the problem as "proved (Lean)". That refers to the 2D statement, whose existing Lean proof (https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1121.lean, by Aristotle and Amogh Parab) is restricted to EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2). The higher-dimensional variant has no formal_proof link in the pinned upstream or the current upstream main branch.

results.title: Müller's set avoids sums equal to powers of two and has density 1/2 (Erdős 1136)
results.summary: Let M be the set of natural numbers n such that n ≡ 3·2^i (mod 2^{i+2}) for some i ≥ 0. Then (1) no a, b ∈ M (not necessarily distinct) satisfy a + b = 2^k for any k ≥ 0, and (2) M has natural density 1/2: #(M ∩ [0,b)) / b → 1/2 as b → ∞.
results.notes:
The result is H. Müller, "Über ein additiv-zahlentheoretisches Problem von P. Erdős", Mitt. Math. Ges. Hamburg (2011), 75-78. erdosproblems.com/1136 lists the status "proved (Lean)" (2026-04-19). Earlier Lean proofs exist:
- plby/lean-proofs src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1136.lean (by Aristotle, L. Luccioli and W. van Doorn), which proves the same set is sum-free (`A_sumfree`) and has density 1/2 (`A_density_half`).
- Luccioli's gist on live.lean-lang.org.
- Woett/Lean-files ErdosProblem1136.lean.

results.title: The multiples of 3 avoid sums equal to powers of two and have density 1/3
results.summary: Let A = {n ∈ ℕ : 3 ∣ n}. (i) For all a, b ∈ A (not necessarily distinct) and all k ≥ 0, a + b ≠ 2^k. (ii) A has natural density 1/3: the quantity #(A ∩ [0, b)) / #[0, b) tends to 1/3 as b → ∞. This is the trivial benchmark in Erdős Problem 1136, which asks for a set with lower density greater than 1/3 and the same avoidance property.
results.notes: Erdős Problem 1136 (erdosproblems.com/1136; problems.yaml gives status "proved (Lean)", last updated 2026-04-19). H. Müller, "Über ein additiv-zahlentheoretisches Problem von P. Erdős", Mitt. Math. Ges. Hamburg (2011), 75-78: Müller's set has density 1/2, and density 1/2 is optimal. The density-1/3 example using multiples of 3 is a folklore fact noted as trivial in the upstream docstring. The existing Lean proof at plby/lean-proofs (src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1136.lean) formalizes the main problem, Müller's set and the upper bound, but not the multiples-of-3 variant.

results.title: Sets avoiding sums equal to powers of two have lower density at most 1/2 (Müller)
results.summary: Let A ⊆ ℕ be such that a + b ≠ 2^k for all a, b ∈ A (not necessarily distinct) and all k ≥ 0. Then the lower natural density of A, liminf_{N→∞} |A ∩ [0, N)| / N, is at most 1/2.
results.notes: Müller, Helmut, "Über ein additiv-zahlentheoretisches Problem von P. Erdős", Mitt. Math. Ges. Hamburg (2011), 75-78. Müller proves the existence of a set with density 1/2 and that every such set has density at most 1/2. erdosproblems.com/1136 has status "proved (Lean)" in problems.yaml (formal_status Lean, 2026-04-19). The existing Lean proof is linked from the upstream formal_proof attribute: https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1136.lean (Aristotle, Lorenzo Luccioli, Wouter van Doorn). It contains `sumfree_upperDensity_le_half`, an upper density ≤ 1/2 bound for any power-of-two-sum-free S ⊆ ℕ, and `main_result`. Related formalizations are Luccioli's gist (mathlib v4.28.0) and https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/main/ErdosProblem1136.lean.

results.title: Every n is x² + y² − z² with max(x², y², z²) ≤ n + 2√n
results.summary: For every natural number n there exist natural numbers x, y, z with n = x² + y² − z² (the subtraction is truncated subtraction on ℕ) and x², y², z² ≤ n + 2√n, where √n is the real square root. This is the relaxed form of Erdős Problem 1148, which [Va99] calls "obvious".
results.notes: [Va99] "Some of Paul's favorite problems", the booklet for the conference "Paul Erdős and his mathematics" (Budapest, 1999), calls the n + 2√n relaxation "obvious". The main Erdős 1148 problem (bound ≤ n, for large n) was proved by Chojecki [Ch26], "Bounded Representations by x²+y²−z²" (2026). Its Lean proof is plby/lean-proofs src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos1148.lean at commit 8822f7d, and it covers only the main theorem for large n, not the weaker variant for every n. In erdosproblems.com's problems.yaml, problem 1148 has status "proved (Lean)" and OEIS entries A390380 and A393168. The upstream formal-conjectures file FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/1148.lean has a formal_proof link on erdos_1148 only.

results.title: Erdős 1180, "optimal" variant: false as stated (C_ε grows exponentially in 1/ε, because the constant must cover all primes)
results.summary: For ε > 0 let C(ε) be the least natural number C such that for every prime p and every residue a mod p there is a multiset s of integers n with 1 ≤ n ≤ p^ε and gcd(n,p)=1, |s| ≤ C, and Σ_{n∈s} n^{-1} ≡ a (mod p). If no such C exists, C(ε) = 0 (Lean's sInf ∅ = 0). The upstream statement says: for every δ > 0, C(ε) ≤ ε^{-(1+δ)} for all sufficiently small ε > 0. We prove the negation: there is a δ > 0 (δ = 1 works) such that C(ε) > ε^{-2} for arbitrarily small ε > 0, namely ε = 1/(m+1) for every large m.
results.notes:
Erdős and Graham, Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory (1980), the source of the question. Shparlinski, Arch. Math. (Basel) 2002, pp. 445–448: at most ε⁻³ summands for all p ≥ P(ε). Glibichuk, Mat. Zametki 2006, pp. 384–395: at most ε⁻² summands for all p ≥ P(ε); his covering lemma is the 8XY = F_p result for antisymmetric Y with |X||Y| > p. erdosproblems.com/1180 is marked proved, and its remark that "it may be that C_ε ≤ ε^{-1-o(1)}" is meant for large primes. The upstream formal-conjectures file 1180.lean already notes, in the docstring of variants.shparlinski, that no polynomial bound can hold for all primes. Upstream also links Lean proofs of the main statement and the shparlinski, glibichuk and lower_bound variants (plby/lean-proofs and linrock/math-proofs). The Glibichuk part of this file is adapted from plby/lean-proofs. The "optimal" variant has no prior formal resolution I know of. Its falsity as formalized follows from the small-prime obstruction that the upstream file itself states. - erdosproblems.com/1180. The ε^{-1-o(1)} question is listed there as still open. The page credits Shparlinski with ≪ε^{-3}, Glibichuk with ≪ε^{-2}, and Croot with (log p)^{3+o(1)}.
- [Sh02] I. E. Shparlinski, "On a question of Erdős and Graham", Arch. Math. (Basel) 78 (2002), 445–448.
- [Gl06] A. A. Glibichuk, Mat. Zametki 79 (2006), 384–395 (mathnet.ru mzm2708): N = 8([1/ε+1/2]+1)^2 summands for sufficiently large p.
- Upstream formal-conjectures commit 377

results.title: Erdős Problem 1193 (i): the lower density of {n : 1_A*1_A(n) = g(n)} need not be 0
results.summary: It is not true that for every A ⊆ ℕ and every non-decreasing g : ℕ → ℕ with g(n) > 0 for all n, the set {n ∈ ℕ : 1_A ∗ 1_A(n) = g(n)} has lower natural density 0. Here 1_A ∗ 1_A(n) = #{(a,b) ∈ ℕ² : a + b = n, a ∈ A, b ∈ A} counts ordered representations (with 0 ∈ ℕ). The lower density of S is liminf_{N→∞} #(S ∩ [0,N)) / N.
results.notes: The problem is Erdős Problem #1193 (erdosproblems.com/1193), from P. Erdős, "A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory", Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89–115. The site marks it "solved (Lean)": the literal question is trivially false via A = ℕ, which gives 1_A∗1_A(n) = n+1. The existing Lean formalization is plby/lean-proofs src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1193.lean (Aristotle / Pietro Monticone; forum thread erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/1193#post-5360). It is linked from the upstream variant erdos_1193.variants.sumRep_univ and proves the key identity conv_ind univ n = n+1, but not the density step.

results.title: Erdős Problem 1193 (ii): the upper density of {n : 1_A*1_A(n) = g(n)} need not be bounded away from 1
results.summary: There is no real constant c < 1 such that for every A ⊆ ℕ and every monotone g : ℕ → ℕ with g(n) > 0 for all n, the set {n ∈ ℕ : sumRep A n = g n} has upper density < c. Here sumRep A n is the number of ordered pairs (a, b) ∈ A × A with a + b = n (i.e. 1_A * 1_A(n)), and the upper density of S ⊆ ℕ is limsup_{N→∞} |S ∩ [0, N)| / N.
results.notes: Erdős, P., "A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory", Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115 [Er80]. erdosproblems.com/1193 says the question as stated is trivially "no" because of A = ℕ (1_A*1_A(n) = n+1), and its data file gives the status as "solved (Lean)" (2026-04-13). An existing Lean formalization is linked from the upstream formal_conjectures file: https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1193.lean.

results.title: Erdős 142: no single k-independent asymptotic formula for r_k(N)
results.summary: Let r_k(N) = Set.IsAPOfLengthFree.maxCard k N be the largest size of a subset of {1,...,N} that contains no non-trivial k-term arithmetic progression. The upstream statement says that for every k ∈ ℕ, the sequence N ↦ r_k(N) is asymptotically equivalent (as N → ∞) to erdos_142.answer : ℕ → ℝ, which is one fixed function that does not depend on k. We prove that this fails for every possible choice of that function: ∀ a : ℕ → ℝ, ¬ ∀ k, (fun N => (r k N : ℝ)) ~[atTop] a.
results.notes:
Erdős Problem 142 ($10000 prize) is open. In erdosproblems problems.yaml, entry "142" has status "open" and formal_status "unformalized". The OEIS sequences A003002–A003005 give r_3 through r_6. Known bounds include:
- Szemerédi: r_k(N) = o(N).
- Behrend and Rankin: lower bounds of the form N·exp(-c(log N)^{1/ℓ}).
- Kelley–Meka (2023) and Bloom–Sisask: r_3(N) ≤ N·exp(-c(log N)^{1/9}).
- Green–Tao: k = 4.
- Leng–Sah–Sawhney (2024): k ≥ 5.

results.title: Erdős 142 (Θ variant): no k-independent order of magnitude for r_k(N)
results.summary: Let r_k(N) = Set.IsAPOfLengthFree.maxCard k N be the largest size of a subset of {1,...,N} that contains no non-trivial k-term arithmetic progression. The upstream statement asks for one function answer : ℕ → ℝ such that for every k ∈ ℕ, (N ↦ r_k(N)) =Θ[atTop] answer. We prove the negation for every possible value of the unknown: for all a : ℕ → ℝ, ¬ ∀ k : ℕ, (fun N => (r k N : ℝ)) =Θ[atTop] a.
results.notes:
Erdős Problem 142 (erdosproblems.com/142, $10000 prize, listed open, OEIS A003002–A003005) asks for the order of magnitude, or an asymptotic formula, of r_k(N), the largest subset of {1,...,N} with no k-term AP.

Known results:
- Szemerédi: r_k(N) = o(N).
- Behrend (k = 3) and Rankin (general k): lower bounds of the form N·exp(−c(log N)^{1/ℓ}).
- Gowers: upper bounds for general k.
- Kelley–Meka (2023), improved by Bloom–Sisask: r_3(N) ≤ N·exp(−c(log N)^{1/12}), later exponent 1/9.
- Green–Tao: bounds for r_4.
- Leng–Sah–Sawhney (2024): r_k(N) ≤ N·exp(−(log log N)^{c_k}).

The order of magnitude of r_k is open for every k ≥ 3.

I know of no previous Lean artifact reporting that `erdos_142.variants.isTheta` (or the sibling `erdos_142`) is false because its answer does not depend on k. - erdosproblems.com/142: open, $10000; it gives order of magnitude as the "more reasonable" goal and cites [Er80], [Va99]. results.title: Erdős 367 (higher full parts): the product of r-full parts beats n^(1+ε) infinitely often

results.title: Projective planes exist for every prime-power order (Erdős 723, existence variant)
results.summary: For every natural number n that is a prime power, there exist types P, L (in Type), a membership (incidence) relation between P and L, Fintype structures on P and L, and a projective plane structure pp on (P, L) whose order is exactly n.
results.notes: The construction of the Desarguesian projective plane PG(2, q) for every prime power q goes back to O. Veblen and W. H. Bussey, "Finite projective geometries", Trans. AMS 7 (1906), 241–259. Standard textbook sources are M. Hall, "Combinatorial Theory", and P. Dembowski, "Finite Geometries" (1968). The open converse is the prime power conjecture (Erdős Problem 723). Related results are Bruck–Ryser (1949), and Lam–Thiel–Swiercz (1989), who showed there is no plane of order 10. In Lean, Mathlib's Combinatorics/Configuration.lean has `Configuration.ofField` (the ProjectivePlane instance on ℙ(K³)) and `ProjectivePlane.card_points`, and LinearAlgebra/Projectivization/Cardinality.lean has `Projectivization.card_of_finrank`. Mathlib does not state the order of ofField or the existence of a plane of every prime-power order, and erdosproblems.com lists 723 as formal_status "unformalized".

results.title: Erdős–Hajnal: infinite chromatic number with independent sets of size m/2 − cm for every c > 1/4
results.summary: For every real c > 1/4 (formally c ∈ ℝ≥0) there is a graph G, on a vertex type in any prescribed universe, with chromatic number ∞, such that every set S of m ≥ 1 vertices contains an independent set I with m/2 − c·m ≤ |I|. The subtraction is truncated subtraction in ℝ≥0.
results.notes:
The problem and its variants:
- Erdős and Hajnal [ErHa67b], "On chromatic graphs", Mat. Lapok (1967), 1–4: graphs of infinite chromatic number in which every m-vertex subgraph has an independent set of size at least m/2 − cm, for any c > 1/4. The classical example is the shift graph with the random-cut argument used here.
- Erdős, Hajnal and Szemerédi [EHS82]: the f(m) = εm case, via a comment by Sellke on erdosproblems.
- Chojecki with GPT-5.5 Pro (ulam.ai/research/erdos750.pdf): the general f → ∞ case.
- Stiebitz [St85], Sachs and Stiebitz [SaSt89], Müller and Stehlík [MuSt19]: the generalised Mycielskian chromatic bound used in that proof.

Existing Lean proofs:
- plby/lean-proofs src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos750.lean, commit 8822f7dd: an unconditional `theorem erdos_750` in formal-conjectures form. It implies variants.c_gt_quarter directly by taking f(m) = c·m.
- Jayyhk/erdos-lean problems/750/Erdos750.lean.
- Shashi456/erdos-formalizations: the conditional version.

results.title: Moon–Moser: a graph on n vertices has at most n − log₂ n + 1 maximal-clique sizes
results.summary: There is a real constant C such that for every n ∈ ℕ and every simple graph G on Fin n, the number of distinct sizes of maximal cliques of G (the ncard of SimpleGraph.cliqueSizes G = {k | ∃ S : Finset, S is a maximal clique, |S| = k}) is at most n − log₂ n + C. Here Real.logb 2 0 = 0. We prove it with C = 1, for every n including n = 0.
results.notes: J. W. Moon and L. Moser, "On cliques in graphs", Israel J. Math. 3 (1965), 23-28. Proves that the number of distinct maximal-clique sizes on n vertices is at most n − ⌊log₂ n⌋, which is the n − log₂ n + O(1) upper bound. J. H. Spencer, "On cliques in graphs", Israel J. Math. 9 (1971), 419-421. Gives the matching lower-bound construction. J. Gao, "On cliques in hypergraphs", arXiv:2510.14804 (2025). Settles the main 3-uniform hypergraph question. erdosproblems.com/775 has status "disproved (Lean)". The existing Lean proof (github.com/plby/lean-proofs src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos775.lean, by Aristotle and L. Luccioli) covers only Gao's hypergraph theorem, not the graph Moon–Moser variant.

results.title: K_{n,n+1} is extremal for Erdős Problem 816
results.summary: For every natural number n, the complete bipartite graph K_{n,n+1} (vertex set Fin n ⊕ Fin (n+1), so 2n+1 vertices) has exactly n^2 + n edges, and it does not contain two distinct vertices u ≠ v with deg u = deg v that are joined by a path of length 3.
results.notes: Erdős Problem 816 (Erdős–Hajnal), erdosproblems.com/816 (status: proved, not marked as Lean). [Er91] Erdős, Problems and results in combinatorial analysis and combinatorial number theory (1991), where K_{n,n+1} is the standard example showing that n^2+n edges do not suffice. [ChMa25] K. Chen and J. Ma, arXiv:2503.19569 (2025), proved the main conjecture and showed that for n ≥ 600, K_{n,n+1} is the unique exception with n^2+n edges. The main theorem has an existing Lean proof at plby/lean-proofs (commit 8822f7d, src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos816.lean, L939), but that file contains no K_{n,n+1} or complete_bipartite lemma. So this variant appears to be formalized here for the first time.

results.title: A 7-regular 3-critical 3-uniform hypergraph on 9 vertices (Erdős Problem 834, chromatic version)
results.summary: There exist n and a 3-uniform hypergraph H on the vertex set {0,…,n−1} such that: (1) H has weak chromatic number exactly 3, meaning it has a vertex 3-coloring with no monochromatic edge but no such coloring with 0, 1 or 2 colors; (2) for every edge e of H, the hypergraph H − e is 2-colorable; (3) for every vertex v, the hypergraph made of the edges of H that avoid v is 2-colorable; and (4) every vertex of {0,…,n−1} lies in at least 7 edges. This is the question of Erdős and Lovász, Erdős Problem 834, part (ii), answered positively by Li [Li25] with a 22-edge example.
results.notes: Erdős Problem 834 (erdosproblems.com/834, from [Er74d, p.282], a problem of Erdős and Lovász). It was solved by R. Li, "On an Erdős–Lovász problem: 3-critical 3-graphs of minimum degree 7", arXiv:2512.24850 (Dec 2025). For the transversal reading, Li shows there are at most 10 edges, so some vertex has degree at most 6, and K_5^(3) shows this is sharp. For the chromatic reading, Li gives an explicit 9-vertex 3-graph with minimum degree 7 (22 edges per the solver) and backs it with witness 2-colorings and a verification script, not a Lean proof. The erdosproblems database (problems.yaml) lists status "solved" (not "(Lean)") and formal_status "unformalized". The formal-conjectures statement Erdos834.erdos_834.parts.ii is still sorry. The solver's witness is a different, 21-edge 7-regular hypergraph on 9 vertices.

results.title: The Johnson graph J(18, 9) has chromatic number at least 11
results.summary: Let J(18, 9) be the Johnson graph. Its vertices are the 9-element subsets of an 18-element set, and two vertices are adjacent when they share exactly 8 elements. Then χ(J(18, 9)) > 9 + 1, so χ(J(18, 9)) ≥ 11. This is the case k = 9 of Erdős Problem 835, which asks whether χ(J(2k, k)) = k + 1 for some k > 2.
results.notes: Erdős Problem 835 (erdosproblems.com/835). problems.yaml lists its status as "verifiable" and its formal_status as "unformalized"; there is no "(Lean)" marker. The general question stays open, but the k = 9 case is known. The odd-k lower bound χ(J(2k,k)) > k+1 follows from Johnson's bound for constant-weight codes (S. M. Johnson, 1962) through α(J(2k,k)) ≤ A(2k,4,k). For k = 9 this gives α ≤ 4420 and χ ≥ ⌈48620/4420⌉ = 11. The bound is tabulated on A. E. Brouwer's Johnson-graphs page (aeb.win.tue.nl/graphs/Johnson.html). Ma and Tang (2025, github.com/QuanyuTang/erdos-problem-835) prove χ(J(2k,k)) > k+1 for every k > 2 with k+1 composite, which includes k = 9. No previous sorry-free Lean proof was found: in formal_conjectures, indepNum_johnson_le_johnsonBound is sorry, and every upstream lower-bound statement depends on it or is itself sorry.

results.title: Sieving [N] by half the classes mod 1000 primes below N^{9/10} can leave more than N/10 (Green's Problem 44 refuted as formalized)
results.summary: Green's Open Problem 44 (from Erdős 1980, Section 6, Problem 3): sieve [N] by removing half the residue classes mod p_i, for primes 2 ≤ p_1 < ... < p_1000 < N^{9/10}. Does the remaining set have size at most N/10? The formal statement Green44.green_44 says yes: for all N, all strictly increasing p : Fin 1000 → ℕ of primes with p_999^10 < N^9, and all A_i ⊆ ZMod p_i with |A_i| = ⌊p_i/2⌋, the set {x ∈ [1,N] : x mod p_i ∉ A_i for all i} has 10·|remaining| ≤ N. We prove the negation. Counterexample: N = 100000, p_0 < ... < p_999 the 1000 consecutive primes 20011, ..., 30161, and A_i the upper half {⌈p_i/2⌉, ..., p_i − 1} of the residues mod p_i.

results.title: Zeros of a(3n) for the signed Stern sequence A005590 are exactly the fibbinary numbers
results.summary: Let a : N -> Z be given by a(0)=0, a(1)=1, a(2n)=a(n), a(2n+1)=a(n+1)-a(n) (OEIS A005590). Then for every n >= 0, a(3n)=0 if and only if n is fibbinary (OEIS A003714), i.e. the binary representation of n has no two adjacent 1 bits. This is Ralf Stephan's 2003 conjecture.
results.notes:

results.title: Quet's integrality conjecture for A091817 holds
results.summary: For every prime p >= 3, write H(p-3) = 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/(p-3) = N/D in lowest terms (H(0) = 0/1). Then p divides 2N - 3D. Equivalently, every term a(n) = (2N - 3D)/p of OEIS A091817 (p the (n+1)-th prime, n >= 1) is an integer.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Leroy Quet conjectures that the terms are always integral. This is true for p < 3*10^4. (Entry: (2*numerator(H(p-3)) - 3*denominator(H(p-3)))/p, Bouayoun and Stephan, Mar 07 2004)

Referees: - OEIS A091817 and its history (oeis.org/history?seq=A091817): the conjecture is still stated as open, verified for p < 3*10^4, and has no proof note.
- Classical source: H(p-1) ≡ 0 (mod p) (Wolstenholme 1862; Hardy & Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, Thm 115).
- Explicit reflection congruence H_{p-k} ≡ H_{k-1} (mod p), 1 <= k <= p-1: Z.-W. Sun & L.-L. Zhao, "Arithmetic theory of harmonic numbers (II)", Colloq. Math. 130 (2013), 67-78, arXiv:0911.4433 (proof of (2.2)). Taking k = 3 gives H_{p-3} ≡ 3/2 (mod p), which settles the conjecture at once.
- The same lemma is cited in arXiv:1108.2361 (Lemma 2.1 of its ref. [13]) and arXiv:1803.02966.
- Analogous k = 2 fact in OEIS A064169 (Adamchuk, Jun 09 2006: p divides a(p-2)).
- No prior formalization found:
  - not in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (checked locally at commit c77fdd4);
  - not among the OEIS Open benchmark statements (Adamczewski, arXiv:2608.11941);
  - no other formal proof turned up in searches.

results.title: A115026 has a term greater than 370: a(119) = 371
results.summary: Let F(m) be the sum of d^L over the decimal digits d of m, where L is the number of digits of m (A101337). For n >= 1, a(n) is the smallest element of the cycle that the orbit n, F(n), F(F(n)), ... eventually enters (A115026). Harvey P. Dale conjectured that a(n) <= 370 for all n >= 1. This is false: a(119) = 371.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: no term is greater than 370. - _Harvey P. Dale_, Jun 08 2022"

Referees: OEIS A151543, "Smallest precursor of n-th cycle in the 'Recurring Digital Invariant Variant' problem" (N. J. A. Sloane, May 15 2009, based on an email from Eric Angelini, Feb 18 2009, with a cycle table by Hans Havermann). Its table entry "13 { 119, 1, {371}}" names 119 as the smallest number whose orbit under A101337 ends in the fixed point 371, so a(119) = 371. The same table has "19 { 407, 1, {407}}" and other cycles with minima above 370. Related pre-2022 OEIS entries: A151544 (2009) lists the cycle elements, including 371 and 407. A157714 (Havermann, Mar 2009) lists numbers in cycles of period greater than 1, such as 2929 and 18829. A005188 lists the narcissistic numbers 153, 370, 371, 407, 1634, ...; since 371 is a fixed point, a(371) = 371 > 370 trivially. Angelini's page "A Recurring Digital Invariant Variant" is at cetteadressecomportecinquantesignes.com/RecurDigit.htm, with a cached copy at oeis.org/A151543/a151543.pdf. The A115026 entry itself (revision #12, Jun 08 2022, unchanged upstream) still states the conjecture and has no correction or %E extension. Web searches found no explicit published retraction of Dale's comment. Sources: https://oeis.org/A115026, https://oeis.org/A151543, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narcissistic_number

results.title: ∑_{i=1..n} C(2n-i-1, i-1)/i is never an integer for n > 1 (A175385)
results.summary: For every integer n ≥ 2, the rational number S(n) = ∑_{i=1}^{n} C(2n-i-1, i-1)/i is not an integer. This is the Shevelev–Seidov conjecture from OEIS A175385.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: We conjecture that Sum_{i=1..n} ((1/i)*C(2n-i-1,i-1)) is not an integer for n>1. (Vladimir Shevelev, Zak Seidov, Apr 24 2010)

Referees: OEIS A175386 (cross-reference of A175385), comment by Ralf Stephan, May 25 2026: the conjecture was proved by an autonomous AI agent (AlphaProof Nexus). Lean file: https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results/blob/main/APNOutputs/OEIS/oeis_175386_conjecture_0.lean (theorem target_theorem_0: for n > 1, the denominator of S(n) is not 1; checked, no sorry). Papers: G. Tsoukalas et al., "Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search", arXiv:2605.22763 (May 2026); T. Adamczewski, "OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?", arXiv:2608.11941 (Aug 2026), cited by OEIS for the proof on p. 15, Appendix A. Classical implication: P. S. Bruckman, "Lucas Pseudoprimes Are Odd", Fibonacci Quarterly 32(2) (1994) 155-157 (https://www.mathstat.dal.ca/FQ/Scanned/32-2/bruckman2.pdf). No even composite N has N | L_N − 1, and with 2n·S(n) = L_{2n} − 1 this settles the conjecture. The A175385 entry itself (https://oeis.org/A175385, history up to #14, Mar 2023) records no proof.

results.title: Positivity of the exponential Mertens function (A209802)
results.summary: Let mu_e be the exponential Möbius function (A166234). It is multiplicative with mu_e(p^e) = mu(e), so mu_e(n) = prod_{p | n} mu(v_p(n)). Let a(n) = sum_{k=1}^{n} mu_e(k) (A209802). Then a(n) > 0 for every n >= 1. This is Zumkeller's conjecture in the OEIS entry.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A209802 (Partial sums of exponential Möbius function, A166234): "Analog of Mertens's function, A002321; conjecture: a(n) > 0." (entry by _Reinhard Zumkeller_, Mar 13 2012)

Referees: No explicit resolution of the A209802 conjecture found:
- OEIS A209802 (https://oeis.org/A209802) and its history (https://oeis.org/history?seq=A209802, versions 1-29) still list "conjecture: a(n) > 0"; nothing about a proof is recorded.
- A166234 (exponential Möbius function) and A368405 add nothing on positivity.

Prior results that imply the conjecture at once:
- K. Rogers, "The Schnirelmann density of the squarefree integers", Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 15 (1964) 515-516, doi:10.1090/S0002-9939-1964-0163893-X. It proves Q(n) >= 53n/88 for all n, with equality only at n = 176.
- L. Moser and R. A. MacLeod, "The error term for the squarefree integers", Canad. Math. Bull. 9 (1966), doi:10.4153/CMB-1966-039-4.
- The same bound is recorded in an OEIS A013928 comment (M. Marcus 2012; C. R. Greathouse IV 2016).
- L. Tóth, "On certain arithmetic functions involving exponential divisors, II", Annales Univ. Sci. Budapest. Sect. Comp. 27 (2007) 155-166, arXiv:0708.3557. It gives mu_e taking values in {-1, 0, 1} with mu_e(p) = 1, and the asymptotic sum mu_e(n) = c x + O(x^{1/2} log x) with c about 0.36094. That settles positivity only for large x.

Together these give a(n) >= 2Q(n) - n >= 9n/44 > 0 for all n >= 1.

Also checked, with nothing relevant found:
- Lelechenko, arXiv:1405.7597
- Cao and Zhai, J. Integer Seq. 13 (2010)
- Web, MathOverflow and Math StackExchange searches

results.title: An equiangular decagon with sides in arithmetic progression (A215010)
results.summary: Garcia's conjecture (OEIS A215010) says that hexagons are the only equiangular simple convex polygons whose integer side lengths are the N terms t, t+d, ..., t+(N-1)d (with d ≥ 1) of an arithmetic progression, in some order. Formally: if N ≥ 3, every side t + σ(k)·d is positive, and Σ_k (t + σ(k)d)·exp(2πik/N) = 0 for a permutation σ of Fin N, then N = 6. We prove that this is false. Take N = 10 and t = d = 1, with consecutive sides (1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 2, 3, 6, 7, 10), so σ = (0, 3, 4, 7, 8, 1, 2, 5, 6, 9). This gives an equiangular decagon.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: hexagons are the only simple convex polygons with equal interior angles with such property, due to the fact that cos(Pi/3) = 1/2." Here 'such property' means integer side lengths in arithmetic progression t+m*d, as in the entry name. (entry by _Robin Garcia_, Jul 31 2012)

Referees: Prior refutations, all at least as old as or published soon after Garcia's 2012 conjecture:

(1) OEIS A118887 (H. Pfoertner, May 03 2006). "Number of ways to place n objects with weights 1,...,n evenly spaced around a circle so it balances." T. D. Noe, Sep 13 2005: "Also number of equiangular polygons whose sides are some permutation of 1,2,3,...,n." The data have included a(10)=24, a(12)=732, a(14)=720, a(15)=48 since the first revision in 2006. W. Edwin Clark (Sep 14 2005) proved there are no solutions when n is a prime power. J. Sondow (Oct 17 2013) records that Murray Klamkin proved solutions exist when n is not a prime power, and adds the formula a(A024619(n)) > 0. The problem was proposed by Brendan McKay on the SeqFan mailing list, Sep 12 2005. https://oeis.org/A118887

(2) G. J. Woeginger, "Nothing new about equiangular polygons", Amer. Math. Monthly 120(9) (2013) 849–850, doi:10.4169/amer.math.monthly.120.09.849. Abstract: "We survey results on equiangular n-vertex polygons with edge lengths in arithmetic progression. Such a polygon exists if and only if n has at least two distinct prime factors." This is exactly the A215010 setting, and it gives n = 10, 12, 14, 15, ... as counterexamples.

(3) Supporting references:
- D. Ball, "Equiangular polygons", Math. Gazette 86 (2002) 396–407.
- A. Bernoff, "Bernoff's Puzzler", MuddMath Newsletter 4(1) (2005), p. 10.
- M. Munteanu and L. Munteanu, "Rational equiangular polygons", Applied Math. 4 (2013) 1460–1465, doi:10.4236/am.2013.410197.
- U. Abel, "Coincidence of the barycentre and the geometric centre of weighted points", Math. Gazette (online Oct 2019). It restates the criterion: at least two distinct prime factors.

A215010 itself (history checked through revision #43, Jan 23 2015) never cites any of these, and its conjecture remains uncorrected. I found no earlier formalization in Lean or any other proof assistant.

results.title: Every odd prime is a side of a Heronian triangle (A229159)
results.summary: For every prime p > 2 there are natural numbers x, y, z, A such that x, y, z satisfy the strict triangle inequalities (x < y + z, y < x + z, z < x + y), Heron's formula 16 A^2 = (x+y+z)(-x+y+z)(x-y+z)(x+y-z) holds in Z, and at least one of x, y, z equals p.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: for all prime p > 2 there exists an integer-sided triangle with integer area where at least one side is of length p." (entry by _Michel Lagneau_, Sep 17 2013)

Referees: Classical formula (n, (n^2-1)/2, (n^2+1)/2) for odd n, credited to the Pythagoreans (Proclus, Commentary on Euclid's Elements I.47; H. Eves, An Introduction to the History of Mathematics, sec. 3-4; cf. Euclid, Elements X, Lemma 1 before Prop. 29). OEIS A046079, comment by Richard R. Forberg, May 31 2013: "For odd n: L = (n^2-1)/2 and H = L+1". In the same entry, Ant King (Jan 29 2011) notes that for n > 2 the n with exactly one Pythagorean triangle on leg n are the primes and their doubles. OEIS A042965 (Sloane, May 30 2014): the primes that are a difference of two squares are exactly the odd primes. Related: A009004 (short legs of Pythagorean triangles). Mathlib has the Pythagorean triple classification (Mathlib/NumberTheory/PythagoreanTriples.lean) but not this Heronian statement. I found no source that addresses A229159's conjecture directly; it is resolved immediately by the classical formula.

results.title: A262957: Israel's b(n), c(n) are coprime integers and a(n) = b(n)
results.summary: Let cf(n) be the value of 1 - 1/(2 + 1/(3 - 1/(4 + ... (n+1) + (-1)^(n+1)/1))), where the integers 1, ..., n+1 are used, the sign after k is (-1)^k, and the innermost tail is 1. Let a(n) be the numerator of cf(n) in lowest terms. Robert Israel defined b and c by b(1)=2, b(2)=3, c(1)=3, c(2)=5 and, for both, x(n+1) = (((-1)^n(n-1) + n(n+2)) x(n) - (1 + (-1)^n(n+1)) x(n-1)) / (n - (-1)^n). Claim (Israel's conjecture, OEIS A262957): for every n >= 1, b(n) and c(n) are integers with gcd(b(n), c(n)) = 1, and a(n) = b(n).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: b(n) and c(n) are coprime for all n, so that a(n) = b(n). I have verified this for n <= 10000. - _Robert Israel_, Dec 22 2015 [b(1)=2, b(2)=3, c(1)=3, c(2)=5, b(n+1) = (((-1)^n*(n-1)+n*(n+2))*b(n) - (1+(-1)^n*(n+1))*b(n-1))/(n-(-1)^n), same recurrence for c]

Referees: OEIS A262957 (local mirror, rev #80, Mar 2025): Robert Israel's comment of Dec 22 2015 states the conjecture, verified for n <= 10000, and it is still listed as open. Peter Bala, "A note on A262957 and A263295" (Dec 24 2015, linked from the OEIS entry): proves the simple continued fraction expansion [0;1,1,2,1,3,4,1,5,6,...] of the limit, but not Israel's recurrence or the coprimality. The cross-referenced entries A263295, A346590, A244279 and A244280 contain no proof. A262957 is absent from Tom Adamczewski, "OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?", arXiv:2608.11941 (2026), and from the epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems and LeanOpenProblems-results repositories. Web searches of arXiv, MathOverflow, Math StackExchange and SeqFan found no prior resolution. The proof uses the classical determinant identity for continued-fraction convergents (p_{k+1}q_k - p_k q_{k+1} = ±1).

results.title: Lang's conjecture a(n) = A250400(n+1)/(n+1) for A294512 fails at n = 164
results.summary: Let V(n) = sum_{k=0}^{n} 1/((k+1)(3k+1)) and let a(n) be the denominator of V(n) in lowest terms (OEIS A294512). Let A250400(m) be the numerator, in lowest terms, of the harmonic mean m / sum_{j=1}^{m} 1/(j(3j-2)) of the first m octagonal numbers. Lang's conjecture (A294512, FORMULA, 2017) says that A250400(n+1)/(n+1) = a(n) in Q for every n >= 0. This is false. The first failure is at n = 164, where A250400(165)/165 = a(164)/11.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A294512 (Denominators of partial sums of the reciprocals of octagonal numbers), FORMULA: "a(n) = A250400(n+1)/(n+1), n >= 0. [conjecture]." (entry by _Wolfdieter Lang_, Nov 01 2017). Companion A294513 (Lang, Nov 02 2017): "a(n) = 2*A250327(n+1)/(n+1) [conjecture]."

Referees: OEIS A294512 (W. Lang, Nov 01 2017; history #1-#13, last edit Nov 12 2017, formula "a(n) = A250400(n+1)/(n+1), n >= 0. [conjecture]" still present). OEIS A250401 (C. Barker 2014; Lang comment Nov 01 2017 conditional on "n+1 divides A250400(n+1)", still present, history #1-#19). OEIS A250400 (C. Barker, Nov 21 2014, b-file n=1..1000, which contains A250400(165) = 15*a(164)). Sibling Lang conjectures in A294513, A294515 are unresolved there too. Not in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (FormalConjectures/OEIS); not in Tsoukalas et al. / Epoch OEIS Open (arXiv 2608.11941; github.com/epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems-results; SeqFan thread "Language models resolving OEIS conjectures", Aug 2026). No SeqFan, MathOverflow, MSE or arXiv discussion found. Independent check: the failures for n < 3000 are exactly n = 164 (gcd 11) and n = 2413 (gcd 17).

results.title: Domino-tileable Young diagrams are exactly the colour-balanced ones (A300789)
results.summary: For every integer partition y = (y_1 >= y_2 >= ... >= y_m), the Young diagram of y can be tiled by dominoes if and only if the number of odd parts in even positions equals the number of odd parts in odd positions. So the Heinz numbers of domino-tileable partitions (A300789) are exactly the Heinz numbers of partitions whose odd parts appear as often in even as in odd positions. Equivalently, a(n) = b(n) for all n >= 1, where a(n) and b(n) are the n-th smallest Heinz numbers of the two classes.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %C A300789 This sequence is conjectured to be the Heinz numbers of integer partitions in which the odd parts appear as many times in even as in odd positions.  (_Gus Wiseman_, Mar 12 2018)

Referees: Already known, so the Lean proof is a first formalization, not a new result:
- Classical 2-core / beta-number theory. I.G. Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials (2nd ed. 1995), Ch. I §1 Ex. 8, pp. 12-15: the r-core is empty iff the beta-numbers are equidistributed mod r. D.E. Littlewood, Modular representations of symmetric groups, Proc. Roy. Soc. A 209 (1951) 333-353.
- Explicit statement of the parity form. S.P. Albion, "Proof of some Littlewood identities conjectured by Lee, Rains and Warnaar", arXiv:2108.12766, Lemma 2.1: empty 2-core (i.e. domino-tileable) iff {lambda_i + 2n - i} has n even and n odd elements, which is equivalent to the A300789 parity condition.
- Black = white criterion for Young diagrams. Codeforces Round 609 editorial, problem 1268B/1269D "Domino for Young" (Dec 2019, codeforces.com/blog/entry/72358).
- OEIS. A304710 (A. P. Heinz, May 2018) states the equivalence as fact: "number of partitions of 2n where the number of odd parts in even positions differs from the number of odd parts in odd positions". A000712 has Meeussen's 2013 comment and Karlsson's Dec 2025 comment. Heinz's Maple program and b-file for A300789 use the criterion.
- The A300789 entry itself (rev #11, May 22 2018, local mirror = GitHub) still says "conjectured" and has no %E updates.

results.title: Odd terms of A323695 occur only at n = k(k+2)
results.summary: Let a(N) be the coefficient of x^N in Sum_{m>=0} x^m (1 - x^(m+1))^m / (1 + x^(m+1))^(m+1) (OEIS A323695, offset 0). If a(n) is odd, then n = k(k+2) for some natural number k. Equivalently, if a(n) is odd then n + 1 is a perfect square.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A323695 (G.f.: Sum_{n>=0} x^n (1 - x^(n+1))^n/(1 + x^(n+1))^(n+1)): "Odd terms occur only at n = k*(k+2) for k >= 0 (conjecture);" (_Paul D. Hanna_, Feb 23 2019). A324300 (G.f.: Sum_{n>=0} x^n (x^(n+1)+i)^n/(1 + i x^(n+1))^(n+1)): "Odd terms occur only at n = k*(k+2) for k >= 0 (conjecture);" (Hanna, Feb 21 2019).

Referees: OEIS A323695 (Hanna, Feb 23 2019; still labeled "(conjecture)" at rev #24, Dec 15 2024; history checked) and its cross-references A323696, A324300 (same conjecture for an i-variant, also unproved), A323675 and A323680. Sibling results proved by others, which do not cover A323695: A325046, odd terms iff N = m(m+1), in S. Fried, "Further proofs of conjectures from the OEIS", arXiv:2607.24832 (Thm 50), also in google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results; A323557, odd terms at r(r+1), in T. Adamczewski, "OEIS Open", arXiv:2608.11941 and AlphaProof Nexus (Tsoukalas et al.). A323695 is in neither google-deepmind/formal-conjectures nor epoch-research/LeanOpenProblems. It is not mentioned in Fried's arXiv:2410.07237 (JIS 25.4.3), JIS 26.1.8 or arXiv:2606.09913. MathOverflow, Math StackExchange and SeqFan searches found nothing.

results.title: A326602: a(n) is odd iff n is a square
results.summary: Let A(x) = Sum_{n>=0} (x^(2n-1)+1)^n x^n / (1+x^(2n+1))^(n+1) in Z[[x]] (the n=0 summand is 1/(1+x)), and let a(n) = [x^(2n)] A(x). Then for every n >= 0, a(n) is odd if and only if n is a perfect square (n = k^2 for some k >= 0, so 0 counts as a square).
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: A326602 (G.f.: Sum_{n>=0} (x^(2n-1)+1)^n x^n/(1+x^(2n+1))^(n+1), an even function; a(n) = [x^(2n)]): "a(n) is odd iff n is square (conjecture)." (_Paul D. Hanna_, Aug 08 2019). Same family: A323689 (Sum (x^n+i)^n/(1+i x^n)^(n+1)): "Odd terms occur only at n = k^2 for k >= 0 (conjecture);" (Hanna, Feb 14 2019); A323675 (Sum x^n (x^n+i)^n/(1+i x^(n+1))^(n+1)): "It appears that odd terms occur only at n*(n+1)" (Hanna, Feb 10 2019); A323690 (Sum (x^(n+1)+i)^n/(1+i x^n)^(n+1)): "the first column consists of all the odd terms" (triangle rows start at n(n+1)) (Hanna, Feb 13 2019).

Referees: No prior resolution of A326602 found.
- OEIS A326602 (local mirror and upstream oeisdata) is still at revision #19, Aug 11 2019, and still says "a(n) is odd iff n is square (conjecture)". No later edits or proof links.

Closest prior work (same involution or parity method, different sequences):
- A323557 (odd terms only at n(n+1)): proved by AlphaProof Nexus (github.com/google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results, APNOutputs/OEIS/oeis_323557_conjecture_0.lean) and in T. Adamczewski, "OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?", arXiv:2608.11941, Appendix A. Also R. Stephan's comment of Jun 01 2026 on A323557.
- A325046: S. Fried, "Proof of a conjecture stated in A325046" (OEIS a325046.pdf, 2025), and "Further proofs of conjectures from the OEIS", arXiv:2607.24832, Sec. 3.8 / Thm 50.

Neither arXiv paper mentions A326602, and A326602 is absent from google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, so it was not in the Tsoukalas et al. or OEIS Open benchmark sets.

results.title: Repunit residues: a(n) = n - 1 exactly for long period primes
results.summary: For n >= 1 let a(n) be the number of distinct values R_k mod n for 1 <= k <= n, where R_k = (10^k - 1)/9 is the k-th repunit. Then a(n) = n - 1 if and only if n is a long period prime (A006883): n is prime and either n = 2 or the multiplicative order of 10 modulo n is n - 1.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: a(n) = n-1 if and only if n is a long period prime (A006883), that is, n is a prime and the decimal expansion of 1/n has period n-1. (entry by _Sen-Peng Eu_, May 19 2020)

Referees: OEIS A335012 (Sen-Peng Eu, May 19 2020): the current revision #31 (Mar 12 2026) still lists this as a conjecture, with no %E line recording a resolution. In the same entry, Robert Israel's comment (Jun 25 2020) gives a(n) = A084680(n), the order of 10 mod n, when gcd(n,30) = 1. That implicitly settles the coprime-to-30 case but not n divisible by 2, 3 or 5. Cross-references: A006883 (long period primes, including 2) and A084680; neither mentions a proof. Background only: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repunit (pigeonhole argument that some repunit is a multiple of n; R_k ≡ k mod 3), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_reptend_prime, https://mathworld.wolfram.com/FullReptendPrime.html. Web searches of arXiv, MathOverflow, Math StackExchange, SeqFan and the Google index found no earlier proof or counterexample.

results.title: A338885: the smallest number in row 655 is 104, not A228286(655) = 115
results.summary: Kagey's conjecture in OEIS A338885 says that for every n ≥ 2, the smallest k for which a diagonal lattice rectangle (integer vertices, no side parallel to the x-axis) lies in the n X k box [0,n]×[0,k] and touches all four of its sides is A228286(n) = min{x + y*z : x, y, z ≥ 1, x*y + z = n}. This is false. For n = 655, the value k = 104 is in the row, but A228286(655) = 115 ≥ 105. So A228286(655) is not the least element of row 655.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "Conjecture: The smallest number in the n-th row is A228286(n)." (entry by _Peter Kagey_, Nov 14 2020; a second conjecture in the same entry, "The largest number in the n-th row is A033638(n)", is true; see approach)

Referees: I found no prior resolution.
- OEIS A338885 (Kagey, Nov 14 2020): I checked both the local mirror and the latest raw oeisdata version (rev #22, Sep 11 2021). The conjecture is still listed, with no counterexample noted, and the b-file covers only rows 2..101.
- Cross-references (local mirror): A228286, A228287, A228288, A338886, A338887, A033638, A085582, A113751. None of them mentions a resolution.
- Code Golf SE question 213754 "Rectangles in rectangles", read via the Stack Exchange API: neither the answers nor the comments mention the conjecture.
- Web searches (OEIS/A338885, Kagey, SeqFan, the min x+yz / ab+cd formulations, ARML 2013) turned up nothing relevant.
- Independent computation: n = 655 is the smallest counterexample (row min 104 vs A228286 = 115). Further counterexamples are at n = 845, 909 and 1019 for n <= 1200.

results.title: A344710: non-obtuse lattice triangles with sides >= sqrt(n) have |det| > (sqrt 3 / 2) n
results.summary: For every n >= 1, let a(n) be the least value of |det(B-A, C-A)| (twice the area) over lattice triangles ABC in Z^2 that are non-degenerate and non-obtuse and have all three squared side lengths >= n. Then sqrt(3/4) * n < a(n). This is Waldmann's conjectured inequality in OEIS A344710.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Formula: "a(n) > sqrt(3/4)*n (conjectured)." Comment: "Conjectured next terms (from the conjectured inequality a(n) > sqrt(3/4)*n) are a(50,...,64) ?= 45, 48, 48, 52, 55, 55, 55, 55, 55, 56, 56, 56, 56, 56, 56." (entry by _Jonathan F. Waldmann_, May 26 2021). A344845 has the same inequality a(n) > sqrt(3/4)*m (conjectured), by the same author, May 29 2021.

Referees: A. Mazel, I. Stuhl, Y. Suhov, "High-density hard-core model on Z^2 and norm equations in ring Z[...]", arXiv:1909.11648 (v1 25 Sep 2019; v3 22 Jun 2023). Lemma 3.4.4, eq. (3.1): sqrt(3)D^2/2 < S(D) < sqrt(3)D^2/2 + sqrt(2)D. S(D) is twice the minimal area of non-obtuse Z^2-triangles with sides >= D, so A344710(n) = S(sqrt n). The paper calls the lower bound "obvious". D. Krachun, "Triangles on Z^2 and sliding phenomenon" / "Extreme Gibbs measures for high-density hard-core model on Z^2", arXiv:1912.07566 (Dec 2019 / Jun 2020). Definition 2.1 gives the same S(D) for all D > 0, and Theorem 2 gives S(D) = (sqrt3/2)D^2 + O(D^{4/5}). The underlying inequality is the classical one: a non-obtuse triangle with all sides >= D has area >= (sqrt3/4)D^2, since area = (1/2)ab sin C with the largest angle C in [60,90] degrees. Equality would need an equilateral lattice triangle, and Z^2 has none. OEIS A344710 and A344845 (local mirror and GitHub, revisions #84/#52 of Feb 2022) still list the inequality as conjectured.

results.title: A348484: no two squares two steps apart; the conjectured formula holds
results.summary: For every n >= 1, let a(n) be the largest number of squares you can choose on an n x n board so that no two chosen squares are exactly two steps apart in the same row or in the same column. Then a(n) = n^2/2 if n ≡ 0 (mod 4), a(n) = (n^2+1)/2 if n is odd, and a(n) = n^2/2 + 2 if n ≡ 2 (mod 4). (This is Yang Hong's conjecture in OEIS A348484.)
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: %F A348484 Conjectures: a(n) = n^2/2 for n == 0 (mod 4). a(n) = (n^2 + 1)/2 for n == 1 or 3 (mod 4). a(n) = n^2/2 + 2 for n == 2 (mod 4).  (Entry by _Yang Hong_, Oct 20 2021; last edit #33, Dec 06 2022.)

Referees: OEIS A348484 (Yang Hong, Oct 20 2021; latest revision #33, Dec 06 2022) still marks the formulas as "Conjectures". R. J. Mathar's Dec 2022 comment gives a 2×2-block checkerboard construction. Its g.f. -x(1+2x-2x^2+2x^3+x^4)/((1+x)(1+x^2)(x-1)^3) matches the conjectured values, but he states it only as a lower bound. Cross-reference: A048716 (the 1-D row condition, k AND 4k = 0). I found no published or online proof of the upper bound on arXiv, Math StackExchange, MathOverflow, SeqFan or general web search. The result does follow directly from the standard fact that a grid graph P_a□P_b has independence number ⌈ab/2⌉, because the "two apart" graph is a disjoint union of four such grids.

results.title: OEIS A362086: every denominator of 1/(2-3/(3-4/(...(n-1)-n/(-3)))) except 9 is 1 or a prime
results.summary: For n >= 3 let a(n) be the reduced denominator of 1/(2 - 3/(3 - 4/(4 - ... ((n-1) - n/(-3))))), evaluated in Q from the inside out. Then for every n >= 3 with a(n) != 9, a(n) is 1 or a prime. (Mohammed Bouras's conjecture; the value 9 occurs at n = 5.)
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: Conjecture: Except for 9, every term of this sequence is either a prime or 1. (Mohammed Bouras, May 28 2023)

Referees: OEIS A362086 (local mirror, revision #35, May 09 2024): "Conjecture: Except for 9, every term of this sequence is either a prime or 1." No proof is recorded. Related prior work, none of which settles A362086:

results.title: OEIS A363482: apart from 49, every denominator of 1/(2-3/(3-4/(...(n-1)-n/(-5)))) is 1 or a prime
results.summary: For n >= 3 let t_n = -5 and t_k = k - (k+1)/t_{k+1} for k = n-1, ..., 2. Let a(n) be the denominator, in lowest terms, of 1/t_2 = 1/(2-3/(3-4/(...(n-1)-n/(-5)))). Then for every n >= 3, either a(n) = 49, or a(n) = 1, or a(n) is prime. This is Bouras' conjecture (2023). The value 49 occurs only at n = 6.
results.notes:

results.title: A375522: S2(n) - S1(n) = 1 fails at n = 42 (the difference is 5)
results.summary: Let p_k be the k-th prime. Define s(0) = 0 and s(k) = s(k-1) + 1/(p_k b(k)), where b(k) = 1 + floor(1/((1 - s(k-1)) p_k)) (this is A375781). Write s(n) = S1(n)/S2(n) in lowest terms (S2 = A375522, S1 = A375521). Sigrist and Sloane conjectured that S2(n) - S1(n) = 1 for every n >= 1 except n = 4 and n = 6. This is false: S2(42) - S1(42) = 5. Lean: theorem result : ¬ statement.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: The differences S2(n) - S1(n) are surprisingly small: for n = 1,2,...,34 the values S2(n) - S1(n) are: 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1, ..., 1 suggesting the conjecture that they are always 1 except for n = 4 and 6 (compare the Theorem in A374983). (Rémy Sigrist and N. J. A. Sloane, Aug 30 2024)

Referees: The conjecture is in OEIS A375522 (R. Sigrist and N. J. A. Sloane, Aug 30 2024; comment added Aug 31 2024; current revision #25, Apr 22 2025). It is restated as still open ("it seems") in A375528 (Sloane, Sep/Oct 2024). Related: A375521, A375781, A374983/A375516 (harmonic analogue, proved by Sigrist), and Sloane, "A Nasty Surprise in a Sequence and Other OEIS Stories", Rutgers Experimental Math Seminar, Oct 10 2024 (slides list these sequences and a general Conjecture 4, with no counterexample). results.title: The 1089-trick map has two 9-digit fixed points (A393794 uniqueness conjecture is false)
results.summary: Let rev(m) be the decimal reversal of m (leading zeros dropped), and let T(x) = D + rev(D) with D = |x - rev(x)|. Havenaar's conjecture in A393794 says that for every n >= 1, a(n) = 110*(10^(n+1) - 1) is the only fixed point of T with exactly n+4 decimal digits. This is false. For n = 5, x = 108910890 has 9 digits and satisfies T(x) = x, but x is not a(5) = 109999890.
results.notes:
Conjecture as stated in OEIS: "a(n) is the unique fixed point of the 1089-trick map T among all (n+4)-digit numbers (verified exhaustively for n = 1..4; conjectured for all n >= 1)." (comment in A393794, entry by _Remco Havenaar_, Feb 27 2026; the entry names the sequence 'Fixed points of the 1089-trick map' and gives a(n) = 110*(10^(n+1)-1))

Referees: OEIS A393794 (Havenaar, Feb 27 2026; #19, Mar 10 2026, no correction as of GitHub oeisdata mirror). OEIS A001232 (numbers k with 9k = rev k; includes non-primitive 10891089; structure theorem by D. W. Wilson 1997 and M. F. Hasler 2022), from which 10*A001232 ⊂ Fix(T) follows trivially. R. Havenaar, SYNTRIAD/digit-dynamics GitHub repo (initial commit 2026-03-09): papers/paper_A.tex still states the uniqueness conjecture, while data/results_export.json experiment id 10 (truc_1089, 7-digit domain, 2026-02-25) lists 108910890 among T's fixed points without remark. Neither source states the contradiction. Y. Almirantis and W. Li, arXiv:2408.02527 and arXiv:2410.11784 study related reversal maps but not this T. No published refutation found.

results.title: No odd n with a(n) > 1 has b^n ≡ b^{a(n)} (mod n) for all b (OEIS A051903)
results.summary: Let a(n) be the largest exponent in the prime factorization of n (OEIS A051903; a(1) = 0). Thomas Ordowski (Dec 2019) asked: are there odd numbers n with a(n) > 1 and b^n ≡ b^{a(n)} (mod n) for every natural number b? The upstream formal statement says such an n exists. We prove its negation: there is no odd n with a(n) > 1 such that b^n ≡ b^{a(n)} (mod n) for all b ∈ ℕ.

results.title: An odd n with a(n) > 1 and 2^n ≡ 2^{a(n)} (mod n), where a(n) is the largest prime exponent of n (OEIS A051903, Ordowski)
results.summary: Let a(n) be the largest exponent in the prime factorization of n (OEIS A051903). Ordowski (Dec 2019) asked whether some odd n has a(n) > 1 and 2^n ≡ 2^{a(n)} (mod n). The answer is yes. The formal statement is ∃ n : ℕ, Odd n ∧ 1 < a n ∧ 2 ^ n ≡ 2 ^ (a n) [MOD n], with a n defined as the foldr max of the multiplicities over n.primeFactorsList. The witness is n = 9687963167864344937 = 7 · 631 · 881 · 3511² · 201961.
results.notes:
- OEIS A051903, https://oeis.org/A051903:
